section_summary: This section documents growing U.S. concern over Japanese acquisition of strategic commodities and equipment between late 1935 and 1937, including oil, scrap iron, metals, chemicals, trucks, aircraft, engines, and machine guns. It combines private inquiries, consular and diplomatic reporting, cross-reference sheets, and internal memoranda about export policy, the Neutrality Act, and the possible military use of ostensibly commercial shipments. The section culminates in reports on Kojiro Matsukata's commodity-purchasing mission and a statistical study showing a sharp rise in American exports to Japan during 1937.

subfiles.title: Interior Department referral of M. Sanford Rice correspondence
subfiles.from: Harry Slattery, Department of the Interior
subfiles.about: Forwards correspondence from M. Sanford Rice for whatever consideration the State Department deems appropriate.
subfiles.summary: Harry Slattery transmits Rice's correspondence from the Interior Department to the State Department. The letter supplies no substantive response but initiates State Department handling of Rice's complaint about exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Japan Plans Ten Tankers
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese construction of fast oil tankers designed for potential wartime service as naval auxiliaries.
subfiles.summary: The clipping says Japan is building at least ten express motor tankers with government subsidies and naval-auxiliary designs. It describes the San Limon Maru and ships for several Japanese firms, including vessels intended to carry raw silk outward and California oil home, and also carries a short item on Australia as a market for American aircraft.

subfiles.title: Rice letter protesting oil shipments to Japan
subfiles.to: Harold L. Ickes, Department of the Interior
subfiles.about: Asks whether Japanese acquisition of oil for military purposes can be stopped or checked.
subfiles.summary: Rice encloses a Los Angeles newspaper clipping and interprets Japanese tanker construction as preparation to obtain oil for the army. He asks the Interior Department whether the activity can be stopped or at least restrained.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to M. Sanford Rice
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Department of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Rice's letter about oil exports to Japan and states that his views have been noted.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton confirms receipt of Rice's December 10 letter through the Interior Department. The response makes no policy commitment and merely records that the Department has noted Rice's views.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on proposed Japanese exploitation of Georgia chromium
subfiles.about: Records an attorney's inquiry about a Japanese proposal to exploit chromium deposits in Georgia and the Navy Department's interest in the transaction.
subfiles.summary: Charles S. Haight reported that a client controlling undeveloped Georgia chromium deposits had received a proposal from an unidentified Japanese party, nominally involving exports to Holland but possibly destined for Japan. Green declined to express a State Department opinion on a private contract, then contacted Admiral Taussig, who asked that Haight provide details to Commander Heim.

subfiles.title: Shipment of Sulphate of Ammonia to Japan
subfiles.from: Milton Patterson Thompson, American Vice Consul, Matanzas
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese shipment of German-produced sulphate of ammonia re-exported from Cuba and evaluates its commercial and possible munitions uses.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese vessel Norfolk Maru carried 2,700 long tons of sulphate of ammonia from Matanzas to Kobe and Yokohama via New Orleans and the Panama Canal. Armour and Company had obtained the German synthetic chemical through a barter arrangement and resold it for cash to Japanese interests. Although the local plant manager believed it would make fertilizer, Thompson noted that the chemical and the cotton to be loaded at New Orleans could also be used in munitions production.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence routing sheets for Japan equipment file
subfiles.from: Military Intelligence Division and Department of State filing offices
subfiles.about: Records staff routing and filing of a Japan-related item under decimal 894.24.
subfiles.summary: These pages contain stamps, classification marks, and a brief routing indication rather than substantive correspondence. They identify the material as concerning Japan and link it to the equipment-and-supplies file.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on Japanese rubber and tin shipments
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a report suggesting that Japan was accumulating rubber and tin for emergencies.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references a Singapore report describing heavy shipments of rubber and tin aboard Japanese vessels bound for Japanese ports. It suggests that the trade may represent a deliberate Japanese government stockpiling plan and gives estimated annual Japanese rubber consumption as about 40,000 tons.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese purchase of a New Caledonia nickel mine
subfiles.from: Sydney despatch by Jay Pierrepont Moffat
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch about a Japanese organization's purchase of a nickel mine in New Caledonia.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references Despatch 114 from Sydney. It identifies the subject as a Pacific Islands Monthly report concerning a Japanese purchase of a New Caledonian nickel property.

subfiles.title: Japanese Purchase of Nickel Mine in New Caledonia
subfiles.from: Jay Pierrepont Moffat, American Consul General, Sydney
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese acquisition of a nickel mine near Koua and plans to improve wharfage for direct ore shipment.
subfiles.summary: Moffat reports that a Japanese organization took over a nickel mine on New Caledonia's eastern coast near Koua. Estimates indicated that 30,000 tons of nickel ore could be extracted, and wharf improvements were planned so Japanese vessels could load it directly.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on Hercules truck-engine manufacturing rights
subfiles.from: Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: References a memorandum about Nissan's effort to obtain Japanese manufacturing rights for a Hercules truck engine formerly sold to the U.S. Army.
subfiles.summary: The note records a telephone call from Mr. Weeks of Hercules Motor Company concerning Japanese engine manufacture. Mr. Kubota of Nissan Jidosha Kaisha sought manufacturing rights for an engine type previously used in U.S. Army two-ton trucks.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to aircraft-engine export license for Yokosuka
subfiles.about: Records the grant of a license to export one aircraft engine to the Japanese Imperial Navy at Yokosuka.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references a letter enclosing Export License No. 632. The license authorized Curtiss-Wright to send one aircraft engine to a Japanese Imperial Navy establishment at Yokosuka.

subfiles.title: White House memorandum transmitting Byrnes's request
subfiles.about: Requests State Department assistance in preparing a reply to John L. Byrnes's oil-company proposal.
subfiles.summary: Early forwards Byrnes's request to the Secretary of State and asks for help drafting an appropriate answer. The memorandum serves as the White House cover for the detailed proposal on the following pages.

subfiles.title: Byrnes proposal for a Japanese-financed oil company
subfiles.about: Proposes a Japanese-financed American and Mexican oil-production, refining, and export enterprise.
subfiles.summary: Byrnes proposes organizing an independent oil company, financed through Japanese bonds, to produce and refine petroleum for Japan while remaining under his operational control. A related Mexican company would refine oil at Ensenada and might jointly develop Mexican petroleum lands with the Mexican government. Byrnes argues that the arrangement would operate only while U.S.-Japanese relations remained friendly and asks whether Washington would object.

subfiles.title: State Department letter to Stephen Early concerning the Byrnes proposal
subfiles.about: Returns Byrnes's letter and encloses a proposed White House response.
subfiles.summary: Hull responds to Early's request for assistance with the Byrnes oil-company proposal. He encloses a draft answer judged suitable for sending to Byrnes and returns the original March 22 letter.

subfiles.title: Draft warning to Byrnes about foreign control of a Mexican oil enterprise
subfiles.from: Stephen Early, draft prepared by Department of State
subfiles.about: Warns that a Japanese-financed oil company operating from Mexico could raise concerns under the principles of the Lodge Resolution.
subfiles.summary: The draft says it is impossible to determine whether the proposed company would give a foreign government practical control for naval or military purposes. It nevertheless warns that establishing a Japanese-financed oil enterprise at a Mexican port would likely be interpreted in some quarters as contrary to U.S. interests.

subfiles.title: Magdalena Bay Resolution
subfiles.about: States U.S. opposition to foreign-controlled possession of strategically situated harbors in the Americas.
subfiles.summary: Senate Resolution No. 341 declares that the United States would view with grave concern foreign-government control, through a corporation or association, of an American harbor capable of threatening U.S. communications or safety. It is supplied as the legal-policy context for the response to Byrnes.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Thompson submachine-gun proposal
subfiles.from: Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: References discussions of selling 3,000 Thompson submachine guns to Japan and licensing their manufacture in the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to a memorandum concerning proposals by Federal Laboratories and Auto-Ordnance. Representatives John Young, W. D. Ryan Jr., and Colonel Walter Mangum discussed a possible Japanese government purchase of 3,000 Thompson guns and a separate Soviet manufacturing license.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese competition for copper and lead concentrates
subfiles.about: References a request that the Guayaquil consulate monitor Japanese competition for copper, lead, and other minerals.
subfiles.summary: The note concerns Japanese purchasing competition for copper and lead concentrates. It records a Commerce Department request for continuing reports from the Consulate General at Guayaquil about those and other mineral markets.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese competition for gold concentrates
subfiles.about: References a request that the Guayaquil consulate monitor Japanese competition for gold ore concentrates and other metals.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records Commerce Department concern about Japanese competition in gold concentrates. It asks that the Guayaquil consulate keep the Department informed about gold and other mineral and metal developments.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese efforts to obtain Jamaican copper
subfiles.about: References concern that a prominent Japanese firm was seeking a Jamaican source of copper concentrates.
subfiles.summary: The note points to a Commerce Department letter about possible Japanese efforts to secure Jamaican copper supplies. It records anxiety among major American consumers about the commercial effects of such a purchase.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department request to monitor Japanese mineral purchases in Jamaica
subfiles.from: Lacey C. Zapf, Department of Commerce
subfiles.to: Wilbur J. Carr, Department of State
subfiles.about: Asks the Kingston consulate to report Japanese attempts to secure Jamaican copper and other mineral supplies.
subfiles.summary: Zapf reports concern that a prominent Japanese firm may be trying to locate a Jamaican copper source and that such a purchase could harm at least two American plants. Citing a recent Japanese contract for an entire Chilean producer's output, he asks that the Kingston consulate monitor Japanese competition in copper and other minerals and metals.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese pursuit of Mexican oil concessions
subfiles.about: References information on Japanese individuals reportedly seeking oil concessions in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to a Standard-Vacuum Oil Company letter. Its subject is the movement of Japanese parties believed to be interested in acquiring Mexican petroleum concessions.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to proposed Alaska Railroad scrap sale to Japan
subfiles.about: References an inquiry about whether the Alaska Railroad could sell scrap iron for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Interior Department sought a decision on a proposed Alaska Railroad sale of scrap iron destined for Japan. The note asks whether the government had any objection to the transaction.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese naval expenditures
subfiles.from: Embassy in Japan, Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: References press information on Japan's planned naval spending and expansion.
subfiles.summary: The note describes a coming Japanese naval program involving capital ships, aircraft carriers, auxiliary vessels, naval aviation, and improved land and sea equipment. It points researchers to Grew's report from Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to unlawful export of a Douglas aircraft to Japan
subfiles.about: References an allegedly unlawful aircraft export intended to provide Japan with a model for domestic seaplane production.
subfiles.summary: The sheet concerns the unlawful export of a Douglas airplane to Japan. It states that the aircraft was ostensibly to serve as a model for building a Japanese fleet of similar seaplanes and references a letter from Colonel William H. Neblett.

subfiles.title: Nixon letter protesting scrap-iron shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Calls presidential attention to continuing shipments of scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Although the OCR is largely illegible, the surviving text and the State Department reply identify the subject as scrap iron being shipped to Japan. Nixon asks that the matter be brought to the President's attention and apparently urges government action.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to J. N. Nixon
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: States that existing law placed no restrictions on exporting scrap iron from the United States.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledges Nixon's January 20 letter, which the White House had referred to the State Department. He says the information has been noted but explains that no existing law restricts American scrap-iron exports.
keywords: Office of Arms and Munitions Control

subfiles.title: Exportation of scrap metals from Cuba to Japan
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Havana
subfiles.about: Reports recent Cuban exports of scrap iron and tin to Japan and the expectation of further shipments.
subfiles.summary: Matthews reports that 5,250,000 kilos of scrap iron and 14,500 kilos of scrap tin had passed through Havana for Japan. The shipments were valued at 27,500 and 350 pesos respectively, and additional consignments were expected.

subfiles.title: Purchase of Scrap Iron in Central America and the West Indies
subfiles.from: Harold M. Collins, American Consul, San José
subfiles.about: Reports Aaron Sendall's regional purchases of scrap iron and Japanese interest in the trade.
subfiles.summary: Aaron Sendall said he had purchased 1,000 tons of Costa Rican government scrap and made similar purchases in Martinique, Jamaica, Nicaragua, and Venezuela. He also spoke with the visiting Japanese minister, who was interested in scrap iron. Collins records Japanese prices, estimated shipping costs from Central America, and Sendall's Costa Rican purchase price.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on circulation of the scrap iron and steel report
subfiles.about: Explains decisions about confidential and congressional distribution of an interdepartmental report on scrap iron and steel.
subfiles.summary: Feis says the Secretary and President reviewed and approved the report before wider circulation. Commerce planned only to show it to interested members of Congress, while State prepared memoranda omitting introductory material, an insufficiently supported price statement, and a paragraph about possible Japanese objections. The full text remained a confidential interdepartmental document, although its underlying information could be used.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Edward Farley telephone call on carrying scrap to Japan
subfiles.about: Records a shipping trustee's inquiry about government action affecting a proposed cargo of scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Edward Farley said the Pacific Coast Line had been offered a late-August contract to carry scrap iron to Japan and wanted guidance about possible government restrictions. Feis declined to advise on business risk but clarified that restrictions on American vessels would require a separate presidential proclamation under Section 2(a) of the Neutrality Act. Farley proposed protecting the company through a contractual hedge clause.

subfiles.title: Senator Bulow's inquiry about manganese exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Requests guidance on whether James J. Madden may sell manganese ore to Japanese companies.
subfiles.summary: Bulow forwards Madden's inquiry about exporting manganese ore to Japan. He asks the Secretary of State for advice that he can pass to Madden and requests return of the enclosed letter.

subfiles.title: Madden inquiry about selling manganese ore to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks whether manganese ore located on the West Coast may legally be sold to Japanese companies.
subfiles.summary: Madden says domestic sales are difficult and overseas purchasers may offer higher prices. Because manganese is a useful war material and Japan was involved in hostilities, he asks whether its export would be prohibited.

subfiles.title: Hull reply on manganese-ore exports
subfiles.about: Advises that no current restriction prevents export of manganese ore to Japan or another foreign country.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that, so far as he is aware, manganese ore may presently be exported to any foreign country. He encloses the fourth edition of International Traffic in Arms to explain laws and regulations covering arms, ammunition, implements of war, and other munitions, and returns Madden's letter.

subfiles.title: White House referral of New Orleans scrap-iron telegram
subfiles.about: Refers A. E. Griffin's telegram about scrap-iron shipments to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: McIntyre respectfully sends the attached communication to State for consideration. The referral places Griffin's protest over Japanese scrap-iron shipments in the Department's equipment-and-supplies file.

subfiles.title: Griffin telegram urging an end to scrap-iron shipments
subfiles.about: Urges the President to stop all scrap-iron shipments to Japan immediately.
subfiles.summary: Griffin wires from New Orleans that he has a firm conviction that scrap-iron exports to Japan should cease at once. The message invokes the views of wireless operators associated with volunteers, although that portion is garbled in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Malayan iron ore and scrap exports to Japan
subfiles.about: References a report on Malaya as a source of iron ore and scrap for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Singapore report No. 220 on Japanese access to Malayan iron ore and scrap. It specifically notes export figures for scrap iron sent from Malaya to Japan and other countries between January 1936 and April 1937.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to proposed Japanese purchase of Lockheed training planes
subfiles.from: Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: References an inquiry about a large Japanese purchase of Lockheed trainers and possible application of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records that Mr. Gross of Lockheed reported Japanese government interest in buying many training aircraft. He asked when the President might apply the Neutrality Act to China and Japan, and the note points to a memorandum of the ensuing conversation.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Lockheed aircraft inquiry and the Neutrality Act
subfiles.about: Explains to Lockheed that the timing of a Neutrality Act proclamation was unknown and that an embargo would immediately cover prior contracts.
subfiles.summary: Gross reported that Japanese government representatives had approached Lockheed about purchasing many training planes. Green refused to predict presidential action, saying only that developments were being watched on a twenty-four-hour basis. He added that if an arms embargo were proclaimed for China and Japan, it would take immediate effect without exemptions for articles already under contract.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Far Eastern Survey release on war-material exports
subfiles.from: American Council, Institute of Pacific Relations
subfiles.about: References a research release on American exports of munitions and war materials to Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to a special release drawn from the Far Eastern Survey research bulletin. Its subject is the scale and character of American munitions and war-material exports to both combatants.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on General Motors truck exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Records General Motors' concern that its Japanese truck exports might support military operations and its interest in voluntary restraint.
subfiles.summary: Edgar Smith said General Motors exported about 10,000 vehicles annually to Japan, mostly trucks, and wanted to comply with any government policy during the Far Eastern conflict. Green explained that no restriction had yet been announced, although Neutrality Act proclamations or additional policies remained possible. Smith said the company was repelled by likely military use and might halt sales, especially if competitors joined a self-denying agreement.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum on voluntary General Motors restraint
subfiles.about: Adds a personal-policy discussion with Edgar Smith about voluntary corporate refusal to support armed conflict.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says Smith gave him substantially the same account recorded by Green. Speaking personally rather than officially, Hornbeck argued that major firms willing to forgo profits could help make war more difficult and set an influential example. Smith replied that General Motors might ultimately benefit from taking such a position.

subfiles.title: Memorandum linking Matsukata's visit to a major crude-oil purchase
subfiles.about: Suggests that Kojiro Matsukata's U.S. visit may concern financing or payment for a large Japanese crude-oil purchase.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes speculation about why Matsukata was coming to the United States as one of four unofficial goodwill visitors. It cites confidential Navy information that the Japanese government, through Matsukata's Issho Company, had bought 500,000 tons of refining crude, much of it from American firms. The writer suggests that Matsukata might be arranging payment or credits for the roughly $4 million transaction.

subfiles.title: Navy Department confidential report on Japanese crude-oil purchase
subfiles.from: William D. Leahy, Department of the Navy
subfiles.about: Transmits intelligence that Japan purchased 500,000 tons of American refining crude for delivery between November 1937 and March 1938.
subfiles.summary: The Navy reports that the Japanese government, acting through the Issho Company, arranged an unusually large purchase exceeding 3.5 million barrels. The supply was divided among Associated Oil, General Petroleum, Union Oil, Standard Oil, and Shell Company of California, with Shell providing half. The source and transaction were to remain strictly confidential.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of Navy petroleum intelligence
subfiles.about: Acknowledges two confidential Navy letters on Japanese oil purchases and petroleum shipments to Vladivostok.
subfiles.summary: The State Department acknowledges intelligence concerning Japanese government purchases of crude oil for delivery from November 1937 through March 1938. It also notes information about negotiations to ship fuel oil and gasoline from the United States to Vladivostok and describes both reports as highly interesting.

subfiles.title: Memorandum Concerning Kojiro Matsukata
subfiles.about: Reviews Matsukata's biography, Soviet oil dealings, and possible search for American commodity credits.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reproduces a biographical sketch of Kojiro Matsukata, including his parliamentary, industrial, shipping, petroleum, and commercial positions. It questions why he must personally visit the United States to buy oil and other commodities unless he hopes to arrange credit. It reviews his 1933 contract for Soviet petroleum from the Baku district, doubts then expressed about his capital and distribution capacity, and broader reports that Japan might seek short-term American financing.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Grew telegram on Matsukata's U.S. mission
subfiles.from: Embassy in Japan, Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: References a conversation in which Matsukata said he was visiting the United States to obtain oil, scrap iron, and trucks.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Matsukata as a principal member of an unofficial Japanese group soon to visit the United States. It says he emphasized Japan's need for commodities, especially oil, and described procurement as the principal purpose of his trip.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram on Matsukata's business mission and Japanese attitudes
subfiles.about: Reports Matsukata's commodity-buying mission, Japanese hostility toward Britain, and his suggestion of unilateral American good offices in the China conflict.
subfiles.summary: Matsukata said he would spend two to six months in major American cities as a businessman seeking oil, scrap iron, trucks, and commercial contacts rather than as an official goodwill envoy. He described a shift in Japanese official sentiment away from Britain and toward the United States, alleging that British diplomatic and naval conduct in China had been offensive. He urged the United States to offer good offices independently, but Grew warned him about adverse American public opinion and concluded that mediation was unlikely to be useful at that time.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese interest in Bahia petroleum deposits
subfiles.about: References a Japanese commission's offer to form a company to exploit petroleum deposits near Bahia.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to a report on an oil field near the city of Bahia. A Japanese commission had shown interest in the deposits and offered to organize a company for their exploitation.

subfiles.title: United States Exports to Japan and China During 1937
subfiles.from: H. S. Patton, Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Analyzes the rapid growth and changing commodity composition of American exports to Japan, China, Hong Kong, and the Kwantung Leased Territory during 1937.
subfiles.summary: The report finds that U.S. exports to Japan rose 70.3 percent in the first nine months of 1937, with especially large increases in scrap iron and steel, copper, petroleum, and trucks, while cotton shipments fell after early stock accumulation and Japanese import controls. It compares these trends with trade to China and Hong Kong, where wartime blockade and shipping risks redirected some commerce and where metal and motor-vehicle exports also rose sharply. A final section compares licensed munitions and aircraft exports, noting that authorized shipments to China exceeded those to Japan but were still small relative to Chinese requirements. The section ends partway through Table II, which supplies monthly quantities for principal commodities.
